Being the neighbour people can actually ask
A letter, a dog walk, a cleared path — the small, unglamorous things that make you someone your street can actually turn to.

Most of us like the idea of being a good neighbour and don't actually know any of the people we'd need to be one for. Not through any real unfriendliness — just the ordinary drift of modern life, where you can live somewhere for years and know almost nobody on your own street. The problem isn't willingness. It's that nobody's ever actually said "here's who I am, here's how to reach me, here's what I'd help with."

So say it. A short letter with your name and number, offering something specific — help with a phone, bins out, a lift somewhere — does more in one page than years of polite nodding on the doorstep. It works because it removes the actual barrier, which isn't whether someone would help, it's whether the person next door feels able to ask a near-stranger. Once you've done that, the smaller stuff gets much easier: walking a dog while someone's laid up, clearing a path before it ices over, noticing the person who eats alone and just... including them next time you're cooking too much anyway.

None of this is dramatic. It's mostly showing up in small, repeatable ways rather than one big gesture — which, if I'm honest, is the whole theory behind everything on this site. Being the neighbour people can actually ask isn't a personality trait. It's just a few specific things, done once, that make the next ten years of living near someone slightly better for both of you.

A few places to start:
Prepared, informed, proactive, reactive — four small habits that add up to a genuinely different relationship with plastic waste.

Most plastic-free advice is either abstract ("reduce your footprint") or all-or-nothing (a full zero-waste lifestyle overhaul). Neither actually changes what you do on a Tuesday. What's worked better for me is thinking about it in four smaller modes, and picking off one at a time rather than trying to do all of it at once.

**Prepared** means the boring, unglamorous setup that makes everything else easier — bin bags folded into every backpack, so a walk can turn into a cleanup without any planning. **Informed** means actually knowing where the plastic sneaks in, which a plastic-free picnic makes obvious fast — you'll be surprised what turns out to be avoidable once you're paying attention, and what turns out to be genuinely hard. **Proactive** and **reactive** are two sides of the same coin: proactive is picking up litter as part of a hike you were doing anyway; reactive is doing it because you happened to walk past a park that needed it.

None of this requires becoming the person who lectures people about straws. It's mostly just carrying the right two-pound item and noticing a bit more than you used to.

How to run a preparedness evening
Most emergency skills take five minutes to learn. Here's how to get a whole evening's worth done with friends instead of alone.

I keep coming back to a slightly uncomfortable fact: almost every genuinely life-saving piece of knowledge on this site takes about five minutes to learn, and almost nobody has actually learned it. Not because it's hard, and not because people don't care — just because it's never quite the moment. There's no natural trigger that makes you sit down and learn the signs of a stroke on a random Tuesday.

So make the moment. A preparedness evening is just that: an excuse to get a few of these five-minute things done at once, with people, instead of hoping you'll get round to them alone. You'd be amazed how much fits into two hours — the FAST stroke test, seizure response, downloading a first aid app, registering as an organ donor, checking what's actually in your car's boot. None of these need a course or a qualification. They need someone to say "let's just do this now" and a bit of shared momentum.

The trick that makes it work is treating it like a normal night in rather than a serious event. Order food, put music on, and work through a short list together — a few five-minute things, and maybe one slightly bigger one like signing up for a proper CPR course as a group activity for another day. Nobody leaves an expert. Everyone leaves knowing a few more things than they did, and — just as importantly — knowing that the people around them know them too.
